topics.title: Validation with Zod, Joi and express-validator
topics.summary: Validate and clean req.body, params and query at the edge using a schema library in a reusable middleware.
topics.description:
**Never trust client input.** Every value in `req.body`, `req.params`, `req.query` and headers must be validated for type, shape, range and length before use. Validate at the edge (middleware) so controllers receive clean data.

### Three popular choices
| Library | Style | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Zod** | schema objects, TypeScript-first | `safeParse`, transforms, coercion, inferred types |
| **Joi** | schema objects | mature, rich rules, `abortEarly: false` |
| **express-validator** | chain of checks per field | `body('email').isEmail()`, built on validator.js |

### Why schemas beat manual `if`s
They describe the contract once, return all errors, **strip unknown fields** (stops mass assignment), coerce types (`"5"` -> `5`) and give consistent messages.

### A reusable `validate` middleware
`validate({ body: schema, query: schema, params: schema })` parses each part; on failure respond `400/422` with the list of issues; on success replace the data with the parsed, cleaned values. Remember that in Express 5 `req.query` is a read-only getter, so store parsed query data on another property such as `req.validated.query` (or `res.locals`).

### Validate more than the body
IDs (`ObjectId` format), pagination numbers, enums for sort fields, file mime types and headers.

### Beyond the schema
Validation checks *shape*; business checks (email already used, stock available) still happen in the service layer. Database constraints (unique index) are the final safety net.
keyPoints: Validate body, params and query in middleware, before controllers
Schema libraries return all errors, coerce types and strip unknown keys
Zod = modern/TypeScript, Joi = mature, express-validator = chain style
In Express 5 do not reassign `req.query`; store parsed data elsewhere
Keep database constraints as the last line of defence
pitfalls: Validating only in React; the API can be called without your UI
Trusting numeric strings without coercion/range checks

examples.title: Zod validate middleware
express-validator version

interview.q: Why validate on the server if the React form already validates?
interview.a: Client checks are only convenience; anyone can call the API directly, so the server must enforce every rule.

interview.q: What does a strict schema protect against?
interview.a: Mass assignment: unknown fields such as role or isAdmin are rejected or stripped instead of reaching the database.

topics.title: Helmet and Rate Limiting
topics.summary: helmet sets safe HTTP security headers; express-rate-limit throttles abuse such as brute-force logins.
topics.description:
### Helmet
**helmet** is a collection of small middleware that set security-related response headers with sensible defaults. One line: `app.use(helmet())`.

| Header | Protects against |
|---|---|
| `Content-Security-Policy` | XSS by restricting where scripts/styles can load from |
| `Strict-Transport-Security` | forces HTTPS |
| `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` | MIME sniffing |
| `X-Frame-Options` / `frame-ancestors` | clickjacking |
| `Referrer-Policy` | leaking URLs to other sites |
| removes `X-Powered-By` | hides the framework |

For a pure JSON API the default CSP is harmless; if you serve a React build from Express you may need to tune CSP directives (images, API origins).

### Rate limiting
A rate limiter counts requests per client (IP or user id) within a time window and answers **429 Too Many Requests** when the limit is exceeded. It reduces brute-force attacks, scraping and accidental overload.

- Apply a general limit to the whole API (for example 100 requests per 15 minutes).
- Apply a **stricter** limit to sensitive routes (`/login`, `/forgot-password`, OTP verification).
- Send standard headers (`RateLimit-*`, `Retry-After`) so clients can back off.
- Behind a proxy set `trust proxy`, otherwise everyone shares the proxy's IP.
- The default store is in memory and per process; with several instances use a shared store such as Redis (`rate-limit-redis`).

### Related defences
Account lockouts, CAPTCHAs, slow-down middleware (`express-slow-down`) and WAF/CDN limits (Cloudflare) at the edge.
keyPoints: `app.use(helmet())` early in the middleware chain
Rate-limit globally and stricter on auth routes
429 + `Retry-After` tells clients to back off
Set `trust proxy` so IPs are real behind proxies
Use a Redis store for multi-instance deployments
pitfalls: Rate limiting by IP without `trust proxy` (all users share one IP)
Per-process memory store in a clustered/Docker-scaled app (limits multiply)
Disabling helmet's CSP because it "breaks things" instead of configuring it

examples.title: helmet and layered limiters
examples.code:
import express from 'express'
import helmet from 'helmet'
import rateLimit from 'express-rate-limit'

const app = express()
app.set('trust proxy', 1)
app.use(helmet())
app.use(express.json())

const apiLimiter = rateLimit({
  windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000,
  limit: 100,                         // 100 requests / 15 min / IP
  standardHeaders: 'draft-7',
  legacyHeaders: false,
  message: { error: 'Too many requests, please try again later' },
})

const loginLimiter = rateLimit({
  windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000,
  limit: 5,
  skipSuccessfulRequests: true,       // only failed attempts count
  message: { error: 'Too many login attempts' },
})

app.use('/api', apiLimiter)
app.post('/api/auth/login', loginLimiter, (req, res) => res.status(401).json({ error: 'Invalid credentials' }))

app.listen(3000)

examples.title: Hitting the limit
examples.code:
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} " -X POST localhost:3000/api/auth/login; done
# 401 401 401 401 401 429

curl -i -X POST localhost:3000/api/auth/login
# HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
# RateLimit: limit=5, remaining=0, reset=900
# {"error":"Too many login attempts"}

interview.a: It sets protective HTTP headers (CSP, HSTS, nosniff, frame protections and more) to reduce common browser-based attacks.
Login endpoints are the main target of brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks, so they need much lower thresholds than normal API routes.

topics.title: CORS: What, Why and How to Configure
topics.summary: Browsers block cross-origin requests unless the server sends CORS headers; configure the cors package with an allow-list.
topics.description:
### The problem
Browsers enforce the **same-origin policy**: a page at `http://localhost:5173` (React) cannot read responses from `http://localhost:3000` (API), because the *origin* (protocol + host + port) differs. **CORS** (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the mechanism by which the **server** opts in by sending headers such as `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`.

CORS is enforced **by browsers only**. curl, Postman and server-to-server calls ignore it, so it is not an authentication mechanism.

### Simple vs preflighted requests
For "non-simple" requests (methods other than GET/POST/HEAD, custom headers like `Authorization`, or `Content-Type: application/json`) the browser first sends an **OPTIONS preflight** asking permission. The server must answer with `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` and the allowed origin. The `cors` package handles it.

### Using the `cors` package
```js
app.use(cors({ origin: 'http://localhost:5173', credentials: true }))
```
- `origin`: string, array, regex or a function (best for allow-lists).
- `credentials: true`: lets the browser send/receive cookies; then `origin` **cannot** be `*`, and the front end must use `credentials: 'include'` (fetch) or `withCredentials: true` (axios).
- `methods`, `allowedHeaders`, `exposedHeaders`, `maxAge` (cache preflight).

### Rules
- Register `cors()` **before** your routes.
- Use an explicit allow-list from an env variable in production.
- Never combine `origin: '*'` with credentials.
- A "CORS error" for a request that failed with 500 or 404 may simply be a missing header on the error response; check the Network tab.
keyPoints: CORS is a browser rule; the server opts in via response headers
Preflight `OPTIONS` happens for JSON, custom headers and non-simple methods
Cookies need `credentials: true` plus a specific origin (not `*`)
Register `cors()` before routes and use an allow-list in production
It does not protect your API from non-browser clients
pitfalls: Forgetting `credentials: 'include'` on the client, so cookies are not sent
Treating CORS as security for the API

examples.title: Allow-list CORS
Browser client

interview.a: An automatic OPTIONS request the browser sends before certain cross-origin requests to ask the server whether the actual method and headers are allowed.

interview.q: Why can't you use Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with cookies?
interview.a: Browsers reject wildcard origins on credentialed requests; the server must echo one specific allowed origin and send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

topics.title: NoSQL Injection, XSS, CSRF and HPP
topics.summary: Understand and block the classic web attacks: operator injection, script injection, forged requests and parameter pollution.
topics.description:
### NoSQL injection
If you pass JSON straight into a query, a client can send operators instead of values:
`{ "email": "a@x.com", "password": { "$ne": "" } }` makes `User.findOne(req.body)` match without a password. Defences: validate that fields are **strings** (Zod/Joi), cast explicitly (`String(req.body.email)`), whitelist fields, and strip keys starting with `$` or containing `.`. Mongoose `sanitizeFilter: true` neutralises operators in filters. The old `express-mongo-sanitize` package assumed a writable `req.query`, so check compatibility with Express 5 or sanitize yourself.

### XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
Attacker-supplied HTML/JS ends up in a page and runs in other users' browsers, stealing tokens. React escapes output by default; danger comes from `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, server-rendered templates with unescaped output, and stored HTML. Defences: escape output, sanitise rich text (`sanitize-html`, DOMPurify), set a Content Security Policy via helmet, use `httpOnly` cookies.

### CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)
A malicious site makes the victim's browser send a request to your API; cookies are attached automatically. It only matters for **cookie-based** auth. Defences: `SameSite=Lax/Strict` cookies, verifying `Origin`/`Referer`, CSRF tokens (double-submit cookie, e.g. `csrf-csrf`; the old `csurf` is deprecated), and requiring a custom header (`X-Requested-With`) that cross-site forms cannot set. Bearer tokens in the `Authorization` header are not affected.

### HPP (HTTP Parameter Pollution)
`?role=user&role=admin` becomes an **array** and can break logic or bypass checks. Validate that expected strings really are strings, or use the `hpp` middleware (check Express 5 support).

### General rule
Treat all input as untrusted, validate strictly, encode on output.
keyPoints: NoSQL injection: reject non-string values; use schema validation and `sanitizeFilter`
XSS: escape/sanitise output, CSP via helmet, httpOnly cookies
CSRF only affects cookie auth: SameSite, Origin check, CSRF token
HPP: repeated params become arrays; validate types
Validate on input, encode on output
pitfalls: Rendering user HTML with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` without sanitising
Assuming CORS prevents CSRF (it does not stop simple form posts)

examples.title: Injection, then fixes
CSRF defence: Origin check + SameSite

interview.q: What is NoSQL injection and how do you prevent it?
interview.a: Sending query operators (like {"$ne": ""}) where a plain value is expected so the query matches unintended documents; prevent it by validating input types and sanitising filters.

interview.q: Does CSRF affect APIs using Authorization Bearer headers?
interview.a: Not really, because browsers do not attach that header automatically; CSRF targets credentials the browser sends by itself, such as cookies.

topics.title: Secrets, Environment Variables and OWASP Checklist
topics.summary: Keep secrets out of code, validate config on startup and walk through an OWASP-based security checklist.
topics.description:
### Secrets and environment variables
API keys, database URLs and JWT secrets must **never** be in source control. Store them in environment variables:
- Local: `.env` (ignored by git) loaded with `node --env-file=.env` or `dotenv`.
- Production: the hosting platform's secret manager (Render/Railway/Vercel settings, AWS Secrets Manager, Docker/Kubernetes secrets).
- Commit a `.env.example` listing the variable **names** only.
- Validate required variables at startup with Zod and fail fast; generate secrets with `node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(48).toString('hex'))"`.
- If a secret is ever committed, **rotate it** - deleting the file does not remove it from git history.

### OWASP Top 10 checklist (API focus)
| Risk | Express action |
|---|---|
| Broken access control | authZ on every route, ownership checks, deny by default |
| Cryptographic failures | HTTPS only, bcrypt/argon2, strong JWT secrets |
| Injection | validated input, parameterised SQL, `sanitizeFilter` |
| Insecure design | rate limits, least privilege, threat modelling |
| Security misconfiguration | helmet, no stack traces in prod, `NODE_ENV=production` |
| Vulnerable components | `npm audit`, Dependabot, lockfile, update regularly |
| Auth failures | strong passwords, rate-limit login, 2FA, short tokens |
| Integrity failures | verify webhook signatures, pin CI dependencies |
| Logging failures | log auth events, never log secrets/passwords |
| SSRF | never fetch user-supplied URLs without an allow-list |

### Extras
Limit body size, disable `X-Powered-By`, secure cookies, set timeouts, run as non-root in Docker, and keep error messages generic.
keyPoints: Secrets live in env vars or a secret manager, never in git
Provide `.env.example`; validate env at startup and fail fast
Rotate any leaked secret immediately
Run `npm audit` and keep dependencies updated
Use the OWASP Top 10 as a recurring review checklist
pitfalls: Committing `.env` or hard-coding a fallback secret (`|| 'secret'`) in code
Logging full request bodies or Authorization headers
Leaving `NODE_ENV` unset in production (verbose errors, slower Express)

# .env.example  (committed - names only, no real values)
NODE_ENV=development
PORT=3000
MONGO_URI=mongodb://localhost:27017/myapp
JWT_ACCESS_SECRET=change-me-to-a-long-random-string
JWT_REFRESH_SECRET=change-me-too
CLIENT_URL=http://localhost:5173

# .gitignore
.env
node_modules/

# generate a strong secret
node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(48).toString('hex'))"

interview.q: What should you do if a secret was committed to Git?
interview.a: Rotate (replace) it immediately, because it remains in history and may already be exposed; then optionally clean history.

interview.q: Name some OWASP API risks and fixes.
interview.a: Broken access control (check ownership, deny by default), injection (validate and parameterise), auth failures (rate limiting, strong hashing, short tokens), misconfiguration (helmet, no stack traces in production).
